implementation_notes: JavaScript makes the seam trivially expressible — a provider module that exposes your own object is the whole thing — which is also why it is skipped. The Node module graph makes the audit easy: any package importing `@aws-sdk/...`, `@google-cloud/...` or an ORM is a dependency, and the ones imported from outside an adapter directory are the problem. Serverless handlers are a special case worth naming: the handler signature itself (`(event, context) => result`) is the provider's contract, so a provider port around the handler is the only seam available. Bundlers do not enforce the boundary, so the only thing that holds it is a lint rule on restricted imports.
idiom_name: provider SDK required straight from domain modules
pitfalls: A provider SDK installed at the top of the dependency tree is importable from anywhere, and nothing stops the import from appearing in domain code.
Lambda-style handler signatures make the provider part of your function's type; without a port, every handler is provider code.
Cloud SDK v3's modular clients are easier to seam than v2 but their shared config (`@aws-sdk/client-config`) is itself a vendor dependency.
